issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. Being alone with women is not a plausible primary trigger for partner violence in a female patient unless there is additional trauma history not represented elsewhere, and military/police uniforms also suggest a different threat context that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: The memory/appraisal pattern centers on guilt and global identity damage, but the selected triggers point toward external threat cues unrelated to intimate-partner violence. This creates a cross-node mismatch: the triggers imply one trauma context, while memory and appraisals imply another.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is not impossible, but in this profile it intensifies the mismatch because the appraisals are extremely global and identity-based while the trigger content is narrow and externally themed in ways not linked to the romantic-partner abuse formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
issues.explanation: Military or police uniforms are not impossible as triggers after intimate partner physical abuse, but in this profile they are hard to justify because no other trigger, memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy item links the trauma to police/military involvement, authority figures, or uniformed responders. This makes the trigger feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
issues.explanation: This item is not impossible, but alongside the more specific interpersonal/self-related profile (self-blame, guilt on recall, being alone with men, body-focused avoidance, belonging nowhere), a global 'completely destroyed' worldview reads broader than the rest of the node and may overstate the appraisal pattern relative to the otherwise relationship- and self-focused presentation.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reflects fear, hypervigilance, avoidance, mistrust, and tension after intimate partner physical abuse. It pulls toward a more disinhibited presentation that is not supported by the trigger, memory, appraisal, or other strategy items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Own Body' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The selected triggers, memories, threats, and appraisals center on interpersonal danger, guilt, and mistrust rather than body-focused trauma responses. This item is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the main formulation compared with the other avoidance item.

vignette:
Malia was a 20-year-old Māori woman who had married young and was working as an interior designer when she first came to treatment, carrying herself with the careful alertness of someone who had learned to read a room before settling into it. A year earlier, while living with her romantic partner, she had experienced repeated physical abuse that culminated in an assault she still struggled to describe in a straight line. She could say that there were loud voices, sudden movements, and the shock of realizing that the person she had trusted was the one hurting her. What stayed most vividly with her was the sound of the blows and the way the fear seemed to fill the whole space at once. Even now, when she tried to speak about it, she often lost the thread partway through, staring down and restarting, as though the words could not hold together long enough to make a complete account. She would begin with one detail, then stop, overwhelmed by a wave of guilt that arrived as soon as she remembered it. She had come to believe, painfully and persistently, that she should have seen it coming, should have left sooner, should have known how to prevent what happened.

In the months that followed, Malia found herself increasingly organized around avoidance. Dark rooms felt wrong to her now, and she would switch on every light in the house rather than stand in a dim hallway or sit alone in the evening shadow. She avoided being alone in a room or a building, and if her husband was out and she was at home, she would leave a television or radio on so the silence would not gather around her. In her work as an interior designer, she noticed herself hesitating in client homes if the lighting was low, especially in unfinished spaces where the shadows made her feel exposed. She could still do the job, but she preferred to keep moving, keep talking, keep herself from being caught in circumstances that reminded her of the event. Her wariness also extended to men she did not know well. Being alone with men now felt unsafe in a way she could not easily explain to other people; she would position herself near open doors, step back when a man entered a room, and arrange meetings so that a colleague or family member might be present. If she saw the offender, or even someone who resembled him in build or posture, her whole body seemed to tighten before she had time to think. She would look down, turn away, or leave quickly, as if distance could restore control.

That sense of danger did not stay in her thoughts alone. Malia described herself as superalert and watchful, always scanning for what might happen next. When she walked to her car, she frequently looked behind her to check whether someone was following her. She did the same in parking lots, in hallways, and in the foyer of apartment buildings, her eyes moving automatically over doorways and reflections. Her body felt constantly tense and ready to react, as though it had never learned that the episode was over. Loud noises were particularly difficult. A slammed door, a dropped metal object, or a sudden bang from a neighboring apartment could make her jolt sharply, shoulders braced and breath held, as if the next strike might follow immediately. She described these moments as happening before her mind caught up, her body reacting with a readiness that left her exhausted afterward.

Her relationship to memory was equally distressing. Sometimes she would suddenly feel the full emotional intensity of what happened without any clear image attached to it, a surge of dread and shame that arrived in her body as much as in her mind. At other times she would recall fragments—the sound, the dark, the sensation of being trapped—but not the full sequence. The missing pieces frustrated her because she wanted to explain herself clearly, especially to her husband, yet she often ended up feeling exposed and ashamed instead. The emotional weight of remembering was closely bound up with guilt; the more she remembered, the more convinced she became that she had somehow failed. She increasingly spoke about her life in global, bleak terms, saying that the trauma had destroyed it, that she no longer belonged anywhere, and that people could not be trusted. Those beliefs had sharpened over time, especially as she noticed how much she kept herself apart from others and how difficult it had become to feel settled in any one place.

By the time she sought help, Malia was living with the quiet strain of these reactions every day. She had not come because she believed herself broken, but because the constant guarding, the avoidance of dark places and solitude, the startle at loud noises, and the fear she felt around men were making ordinary life feel narrow and precarious. She wanted to be able to work without bracing herself, to move through rooms without checking behind her, and to speak about what had happened without losing her words or being flooded by guilt. What frightened her most was the sense that she might never again feel that she belonged anywhere; what she hoped for, more modestly but urgently, was a way to live without feeling as though danger was always just behind her.
